summary: A land of ice and rock in the central Southern Alps: 19 peaks over 3,000 metres, among them New Zealand's highest, the 3,724-metre Aoraki/Mount Cook, and glaciers over 40 per cent of the park. The Hooker Valley Track leads to an iceberg-flecked lake at the mountain's foot, and the tiny alpine village at the end of State Highway 80 is a base for walkers, climbers and stargazers.
story: Glaciers cover 40 per cent of the park, and five great valley systems — the Godley, Murchison, Tasman, Hooker and Mueller — have been carved by them. Haupapa/Tasman Glacier, New Zealand's largest and longest, is 23 kilometres long and up to three wide; under its cover of rock debris the ice is about 600 metres deep near the Hochstetter Icefall. Like glaciers worldwide it is retreating. Tasman Lake, at its foot, did not exist until 1974 and is growing quickly as the ice melts.

There is almost no forest. Instead more than 300 species of plants grow here, among them many mountain buttercups and daisies; the Mount Cook lily, Ranunculus lyallii, is the largest buttercup in the world. About 40 species of birds live in the park. The kea is the most distinctive, while the tiny rock wren/pīwauwau, the only true alpine bird, survives winter in high rock basins. The braided bed of the Tasman River is home to the kakī/black stilt, one of New Zealand's rarest birds.

To Ngāi Tahu, Aoraki is the most sacred of ancestors. In the tradition DOC tells, Aoraki was a young boy in the canoe Te Waka a Aoraki, which ran aground on a reef and tilted; he and his brothers climbed to the high side, and the south wind froze them into the stone of the Southern Alps/Kā Tiritiri o te Moana. The mountain has Tōpuni status, a public symbol of Ngāi Tahu mana whenua, and Ngāi Tahu hold that it is not appropriate to climb onto what is, in effect, the head of an ancestor. Captain J. L. Stokes named it Mount Cook in 1851.

Overgrazing and burning prompted the Government to reserve the Hooker and Mueller valleys in 1885, and the Tasman Valley in 1887. The Rev. W. S. Green came within 20 metres of the summit in 1882; Tom Fyfe, Jack Clarke and George Graham reached it in 1894. After the National Parks Act 1952, the reserves were united as Mount Cook National Park in 1953. On 1 October 1998 the park took the name Aoraki/Mount Cook under the Ngāi Tahu Claims Settlement Act.
howItWorks: Aoraki/Mount Cook is public conservation land run by the Department of Conservation (DOC), and entry is free: the park is managed for its preservation and for freedom of entry and access for public enjoyment, the twin aims of New Zealand's national parks. That may change for overseas visitors. The Government is investigating an access levy for international visitors at four sites, Aoraki/Mount Cook among them; the Conservation Amendment Bill that would allow it was introduced on 7 May 2026, and DOC consulted on the details between June and August 2026. Nothing is charged until the Bill becomes law and regulations follow — check before you go. DOC already charges for parking at White Horse Hill.

The village at the end of SH80 has the DOC visitor centre, a day shelter with toilets and showers, a petrol station and a few places to eat; the nearest supermarkets are in Twizel and Tekapo. White Horse Hill Campground, at the start of the Hooker Valley Track, is DOC's campsite and must be booked. Above the valleys, the park's high huts are serviced alpine huts and club huts for climbers, with radios and a daily 6.45 pm weather check-in. Mueller Hut, on the Mueller Range, must be booked in summer, and hut passes and tickets are not accepted there.

Most of the park is complex avalanche terrain, and avalanches can occur in any season because snow falls year-round up high. Before heading beyond the valley walks, DOC advises checking the New Zealand Avalanche Advisory and asking at the visitor centre. Dogs and other animals are not allowed, there is a permanent fire ban, and recreational drones are banned throughout the park. Rubbish bins are few, so take your waste out; leaving any waste, including human waste, is unacceptable to Ngāi Tahu, because the waters that flow from Aoraki are sacred.

sights.name: Aoraki/Mount Cook
sights.note: New Zealand's highest mountain at 3,724 metres, sacred to Ngāi Tahu as their most revered ancestor. Seen from the Hooker Valley Track, Kea Point and Tasman Glacier View.

sights.name: Hooker Valley Track
sights.note: Ten kilometres return from White Horse Hill to Hooker Lake at the foot of Aoraki, over three swing bridges, one the country's longest at 189 m. Icebergs in summer.

sights.name: Tasman Glacier View and the Blue Lakes
sights.note: Over 300 steps up a moraine wall to a view across Tasman Lake to Haupapa/Tasman Glacier; a side track reaches the first Blue Lake, now green with rainwater.

sights.name: Haupapa/Tasman Glacier
sights.note: New Zealand's largest and longest glacier, 23 km long and up to 3 km wide, its lower reaches covered in rock. Visible from the highway at the park entrance.

sights.name: Kea Point
sights.note: A gentle walk across subalpine grassland to a deck on the Mueller Glacier moraine wall, facing Mount Sefton, the Hooker Valley and Aoraki. Two hours return from the village.

sights.name: Sealy Tarns
sights.note: The 'stairway to heaven': 2,200 steps and 600 metres of climbing to small alpine lakes above the Hooker Valley. No shelter; turn back if north-west weather approaches.

sights.name: Aoraki/Mount Cook National Park Visitor Centre
sights.note: DOC's visitor centre at 1 Larch Grove in the village, with exhibits, an art collection, and advice on huts, weather and avalanche conditions.

entrances: Aoraki/Mount Cook Village, at the end of SH80 — the visitor centre and the Kea Point and Sealy Tarns tracks
White Horse Hill car park and campground, at the end of Hooker Valley Road, 2.5 km from the village — the Hooker Valley Track and the route to Mueller Hut
Tasman Valley car park, at the end of Tasman Valley Road — Tasman Glacier View and the Blue Lakes
planYourVisit.reservations: There is no entry booking. White Horse Hill Campground must be booked and is often full all year; Mueller Hut must be booked from 2 November 2026 to 2 May 2027. From November to March parking at White Horse Hill may be limited between 10 am and 4 pm. The international visitor access levy proposed for Aoraki/Mount Cook is not yet law — check with DOC before you go.
permits: Commercial drone use needs a DOC permit; recreational drones are not allowed anywhere in the park
camping: White Horse Hill Campground: 72 tent sites, treated water, cooking shelter and basic toilets; no power or showers; booking required
Facilities at the campground are reduced from 1 June to 31 August
lodging: Hotels and lodges in Aoraki/Mount Cook Village, among them The Hermitage
Mueller Hut, a 28-bunk serviced alpine hut on the Mueller Range — an alpine route, not a walk
Serviced alpine and club huts for mountaineers higher in the park
seasonalClosures: Snow can close SH80, and access may be limited from June to September — check highway conditions before you go
Large avalanches cross the Ball Hut Road each winter and spring
Snow and ice on the Mueller Hut route from March to November; the Sealy Tarns Track can be extremely icy in winter

weather: Snow falls year-round at high altitude, and avalanches can come down in any season — in summer for climbers up high, and in winter and spring on some park tracks and the Ball Hut Road. Summer is the season for alpine flowers and for icebergs on Hooker and Tasman lakes; it is also the busiest time, especially from Christmas to mid-February, and DOC suggests mid-February to Easter for fewer people. In winter Tasman Lake can freeze, the high tracks turn icy and SH80 may be closed by snow. Bad weather generally arrives from the north-west. With no towns nearby and downcast lighting in the village, the park is one of the best places in New Zealand to see the night sky.
directions: The park is in the central South Island, reached off State Highway 8 at the end of State Highway 80, which runs up the shore of Lake Pukaki. DOC puts the drive at three and a half hours from Queenstown and four and a half from Christchurch; Twizel is about an hour away and Tekapo an hour and a half. The Hooker Valley and Tasman Valley roads turn off SH80 just outside the village.

fees.title: White Horse Hill car park
fees.detail: NZ$25 a day; free if you leave within 20 minutes; overnight parking counts as two days. Card only; locals can buy an annual permit online. Campers with a booking park in the campsite area. As listed by DOC in November 2026.

fees.title: Tasman Valley car park
fees.detail: DOC announced on 16 November 2026 that parking at Tasman Glacier will be charged from December 2026: the first 10 minutes free, NZ$2.50 a half hour or NZ$20 a day. Check before you go.

fees.title: White Horse Hill Campground
fees.detail: Children 5–17 NZ$10, infants free; booked online, with a NZ$10 fee for bookings made by phone or at a visitor centre. As listed by DOC in November 2026.

fees.title: Mueller Hut, 1 October – 30 April
fees.detail: NZ$57 at weekends; from 1 December to 29 February NZ$60 on weekdays and NZ$62 at weekends; NZ$50 from 1 May to 30 September; NZ Alpine Club members NZ$40. Hut passes and tickets are not accepted. As listed by DOC in November 2026.

chronology.text: Captain J. L. Stokes names the mountain Mount Cook, after James Cook.
The Rev. W. S. Green and two Swiss guides climb to within 20 metres of the summit.
The Hooker and Mueller valleys are reserved, the first part of the future park; the Tasman Valley follows in 1887.
Tom Fyfe, Jack Clarke and George Graham make the first ascent of Aoraki/Mount Cook.
A stream breaks out from the Mueller Glacier and damages the original Hermitage.
The Sawyer Stream hydro scheme is built to power The Hermitage; the national grid reaches Mount Cook in 1961.
The reserves are united as Mount Cook National Park under the National Parks Act 1952.
Tasman Lake first appears at the foot of the retreating Tasman Glacier.
With Westland and Fiordland, the park forms New Zealand's first World Heritage Area, later part of Te Wāhipounamu.
The park is renamed Aoraki/Mount Cook National Park on 1 October under the Ngāi Tahu Claims Settlement Act.
A new 189-metre swing bridge, the longest in New Zealand, opens on the Hooker Valley Track in July.

safety: Avalanches can occur in any season. Check the New Zealand Avalanche Advisory, and do not go beyond the outlet of Hooker Lake without avalanche experience.

The Mueller Hut route crosses complex avalanche terrain with no way to avoid exposure when the slopes hold snow; without experience, go up or down only when the danger is low, and be ready to stay longer at the hut.
Never stop in the marked avalanche paths on the Ball Hut Road in winter and spring.
The Sealy Tarns Track is steep, narrow and slippery when snow is present, with no shelter; turn back if bad weather approaches from the north-west. Ice axe and crampons may be needed in winter.
regulations: No dogs or other animals in the national park.
A permanent fire ban applies throughout the park.
Recreational drones are banned everywhere in the park; commercial drone use needs a DOC permit.
Take all rubbish out, and use a pack-it-out method for human waste in alpine areas without toilets.
Park only in marked parking areas in the village and at the car parks.
